extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, policymakers, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for when a patent is eligible for review under AIA §18 (the transitional covered business-method patent proceeding), what prior art may be asserted, who may petition, procedural limits (stays/estoppel), and the scope/exclusions of the statutory definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art that may be raised in a section 18 proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 limits the prior art that can be raised against a first-to-invent patent to prior art that is publicly accessible; pre-AIA §102(b) loss-of-right provisions cannot be asserted in a section 18 proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee and floor managers emphasized that the prior art available in a section 18 proceeding is restricted to what falls within pre-AIA §102(a)'s publicly-available prior-art scope. The limitation was adopted to avoid discovery-intensive, secret-prior-art issues that would be difficult to address in an administrative proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clause (i) and (ii) specification of permissible prior art (statutory text)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subparagraph (C) provides that an anticipation or obviousness challenge may be supported with: (i) prior art described by §102(a) as in effect the day before the AIA effective date; or (ii) prior art that (I) discloses the invention more than 1 year before the U.S. application date and (II) would be described by pre-AIA §102(a) if the disclosure had been made by another before the applicant's invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clause (i) = straightforward reference to pre-AIA §102(a) prior art. Clause (ii) is a hybrid: it combines pre-AIA §102(a)'s substantive scope with an assumption that the material is outside pre-AIA §102(b)'s invention-date-based grace period. Purpose: to capture the universe of pre-AIA §102(b) prior art that is publicly accessible while excluding secret-prior-art and invention-date disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'covered business-method patent' (statutory core)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'covered business method patent' means a patent that claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory definition sets the baseline eligibility for section 18 review: the claimed invention must relate to data processing or other operations tied to a financial product or service and may be claimed as methods or corresponding apparatus. The House added 'or other operations' to broaden scope beyond USPTO class 705.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion for 'patents for technological inventions'
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition explicitly excludes 'patents for technological inventions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Floor statements clarify that the exclusion is intended to cover patents whose novelty turns on a technological innovation over the prior art and that are concerned with a technical problem solved with a technical solution, requiring claims to state the technical features the inventor seeks to protect. Mere recitation of technology (computer hardware, networks, software, memory, storage media, scanners, GUIs, specialized machines, etc.) does not by itself make a patent a 'technological invention.' An 'actual software invention'—i.e., one that is novel as software—would be a technological invention and thus not subject to section 18 review. Conversely, using known technology to implement an abstract business method does not automatically exclude the patent from review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software-related threshold under the technological-invention exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent that recites software elements is not ineligible for review simply because it recites software; to fall within the technological-invention exclusion the invention must be novel as software or plausibly asserted to be novel as software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senators explained that many business-method patents recite software elements but are not 'software inventions' in the sense required by the exclusion. The Office should not rely on mere recitation of technological elements to classify a patent as outside section 18; the patent must colorably appear to be a software (or other technological) invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'financial product or service'
rubrics_metrics.description: A financial product is, at its most basic, an agreement between two parties stipulating movements of money or other consideration now or in the future; to be eligible for section 18 review, patent claims must only be broad enough to cover a financial product or service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senator Schumer listed extensive examples and emphasized that the patent need not recite a specific financial product or service; it is enough that the claims are broad enough to cover one. The definition is not limited to traditional banking—insurance, brokerages, mutual funds, annuities, and other financial companies fall within the scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'practice, administration, or management' of a financial product or service
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'practice, administration or management' is intended to cover ancillary activities related to a financial product or service, not only patents claiming the product or service itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include marketing, customer interfaces, website management and functionality, transmission or management of data, servicing, underwriting, customer communications, and back-office operations (e.g., payment processing, stock clearing). The provision therefore reaches patents that claim activities financial in nature, incidental to financial activity, or complementary to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth expansion via 'or other' and inclusion of 'corresponding apparatus'
rubrics_metrics.description: House amendment changed 'data processing operations' to 'data processing or other operations' and included 'method or corresponding apparatus' in the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The addition of 'or other' broadens coverage beyond class 705 patents. 'Method or corresponding apparatus' is intended to encompass any claim type (method, system, apparatus, GUI claims, data structure claims, Beauregard claims on storage media, Lowry claims, etc.) so that clever drafting cannot avoid PTO review—form should not trump substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file petitions and standing concerns (privy issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: The House allowed additional parties to file a petition for review and expanded the definition of eligible patents; floor debate concerned whether petitioning should be limited (e.g., banks) or open to others, and whether suits against customers or 'privies' could support petitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics worried that adding 'privy' would let companies seek section 18 proceedings based on customers of the petitioner who had been sued or accused of infringement. Supporters noted endorsements from broad trade groups (National Retail Federation, U.S. Chamber) and argued the provision is not tied to one industry. The House changes extended the time and expanded petitioner eligibility to avoid allowing patent holders to delay and evade review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion for stay of copending civil action: special four-factor test and interlocutory appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion for a stay of a copending civil action for infringement is required to be considered under a special four-factor test, and the parties may seek review of the district court's stay decision on interlocutory appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute sets a special four-factor stay test for courts to consider whether to stay an ongoing civil case when a section 18 petition is filed. The existence of interlocutory appellate review of such stays was included in the legislation, signaling attention to coordination between administrative proceedings and civil litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel and PTO consideration of prior court findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a prior district court decision upholding validity may not preclude the PTO from considering the same issues, PTO officials must consider the court's decision and deviate from its findings only to the extent reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senator Leahy indicated that the rule barring the PTO from reconsidering issues previously considered during examination or earlier reexamination remains applicable. He expressed the expectation that the USPTO would not initiate proceedings where the petition does not raise a plausible basis to revisit issues already reasonably resolved by a court, reflecting deference to prior judicial determinations while preserving PTO authority to revisit validity in appropriate circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program effective dates and sunset
rubrics_metrics.description: The new proceeding becomes effective on September 16, 2012 and, absent subsequent legislative extension, the authority to file petitions for review will terminate on September 16, 2020.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute includes an express effective date and a sunset provision (initially eight years after commencement), which were debated and adjusted between Senate and House versions (including arguments to extend the period). The temporal limitation was part of compromises in finalizing section 18.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative purpose: address low-quality business-method patents and provide alternative to litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 was promoted as a relatively cheap alternative to civil litigation to challenge potentially invalid business-method patents and to reduce the burden on courts from low-quality patents (often associated with 'patent trolls').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee report and floor statements cited issuance of poor-quality business-method patents, lack of examiner expertise and prior art, and the international rarity of business-method patents as motivating factors. Proponents emphasized cost-savings and quicker resolution versus expensive litigation; opponents argued about retroactivity, fairness, and impacts on patent holders.
